analysis.one_liner: Requires OSHA to issue an emergency safety standard protecting health care workers from COVID-19 exposure.
analysis.headline: Introduced a week after COVID-19 hit the U.S. health care system, the bill attracted 54 Democratic cosponsors but never got a hearing or vote in any House committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced the Department of Labor to issue, within one month, an enforceable emergency rule requiring hospitals, nursing homes, and other high-risk employers to write and carry out a detailed plan to keep workers from catching COVID-19 on the job — protective equipment, isolation precautions, and infection controls based on CDC guidelines. It would also start work on a permanent standard and tie the rule to Medicare participation for hospitals and nursing homes not already covered by workplace safety law. Instead, the bill sat in three House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care workers — nurses, aides, EMTs, hospital and nursing home staff — who faced infection on the job during the pandemic, plus the patients and public whose safety depends on health care workers staying healthy. The bill would have given them enforceable protections rather than advisory CDC guidance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health care workers and their patients

how_it_helps.text: The bill required the Labor Secretary to issue, within one month, an emergency temporary standard protecting health care employees and other elevated-risk workers from COVID-19 exposure, requiring employers to develop and implement a comprehensive infectious disease exposure control plan [S3].

Each standard had to be at least as protective as the CDC's 2007 isolation precautions guidelines, which are advisory only and not binding on employers, and no less protective than any state-approved workplace safety plan [S3].

Hospitals and skilled nursing facilities not otherwise covered by the Occupational Safety and Health Act would have had to comply with the standards as a condition of Medicare participation, enforceable through existing Medicare compliance mechanisms [S3].

The bill cited hundreds of health care workers already infected or quarantined by March 2020 and surveys finding many facilities inadequately prepared to protect them, and noted that OSHA had suspended its 2009 rulemaking on an infectious disease standard in 2017 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, nursing homes, and other health care employers, who would bear the cost of protective equipment, testing, isolation precautions, and written exposure control plans during a period when many facilities were already under severe financial and staffing strain.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden would have fallen on hospitals and nursing homes within 30 days of enactment, during the early pandemic when many facilities reported shortages of protective equipment and were losing money — the rules could have mandated precautions employers could not immediately supply.

The bill anchored the required precautions to the CDC's 2007 SARS-era guideline and any updates, which critics could argue was a rigid template for a new virus whose transmission characteristics were still being learned; the standard also pre-committed OSHA to a state-plan floor that could exceed federal requirements [S3].

The bill drew no Republican cosponsors, and opponents of a COVID emergency standard generally argued that flexible CDC guidance and voluntary employer programs were better suited to a rapidly evolving outbreak than a fixed enforceable rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were concrete and urgent: health care workers were among the first Americans exposed to COVID-19, with no enforceable federal standard governing their protection, and the bill's own findings document infections, quarantines, and unprepared facilities by March 2020 [S3]. The costs fell on health care employers, some genuinely strained in early 2020, and the 30-day deadline and SARS-era template were legitimate design criticisms. On balance the bill addressed a life-and-death exposure for a workforce that also protects the public, with compliance costs borne by an industry that could have passed much of the cost through. Its weakness was political, not substantive: it drew support only from one party and never got a hearing, let alone a debate over these trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and to a health subcommittee the next day, but none of them ever scheduled a hearing or vote, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott introduced the bill on March 9, 2020, as COVID-19 began spreading through U.S. health care settings [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means committees, and on March 10 to the Health Subcommittee [S5].
No committee took up the bill; there is no hearing, markup, or vote in the action history, and it never reached the House floor [S1][S5].
It ended the Congress without a floor vote, so no COVID-specific emergency safety standard was enacted through this bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, nursing homes, and other health care employers benefited from the bill's death: they never faced a binding federal rule requiring protective equipment, infection controls, and written exposure plans for their workers during the pandemic, and continued operating under advisory CDC guidance instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health care employers, whose costs stayed voluntary

for.name: Rep. Robert C. 'Bobby' Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing OSHA to issue an emergency and permanent COVID-19 worker safety standard.

against.name: House Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: Trump Administration (Department of Labor)
against.what_they_did: Declined to issue an emergency temporary standard for COVID-19 workplace exposure, consistent with its 2017 suspension of OSHA's infectious-disease rulemaking cited in the bill; no executive action filled the gap the bill targeted.

sides.party_line_note: All 54 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record — the only partisan signal is one-sided sponsorship [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have required hospitals to implement and pay for exposure control plans, protective equipment, and isolation precautions for staff, and tied compliance to Medicare participation for hospitals outside OSHA's coverage. Their cost was workers' and patients' protection, so their interest in blocking the bill ran against the public's.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: Skilled nursing facilities not covered by OSHA would have had to meet the standard as a Medicare condition. Long-term care became a center of COVID-19 deaths among both residents and staff, making the protections most consequential there.

industries.industry: Health care workers' unions and safety advocates
industries.note: The bill's findings cite union petitions and surveys as the source of its evidence, and an enforceable standard would have turned unions' demands for protective equipment and infection controls into binding requirements.
